claims.source: Previous studies have shown that one sugar-sensitive GSN in H. armigera is located in each of two lateral sensilla styloconica in the larva (Tang et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 2013), and many sugar-sensitive GSNs are distributed in the numerous contact chemosensilla of antennae (Jiang et al., 2015), tarsi (Blaney and Simmonds, 1990; Zhang et al., 2010), and proboscis (Blaney and Simmonds, 1988) in the adult.
claims.evidence: This is cited from multiple sources.

claims.claim: The lateral sensilla styloconica of H. armigera larvae showed significant unicellular responses to 10 mM sucrose and fucose.
claims.source: The lateral sensilla styloconica showed significant unicellular responses to 10 mM sucrose and fucose, with the firing rates of 169±8.57 and 43±9.78 spikes/s, respectively (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The threshold concentration for larval lateral sensilla styloconica response to sucrose is 0.1 mM.
claims.source: The threshold concentrations for their responses to sucrose and fucose were 0.1 mM and 10 mM, respectively (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The threshold concentration for larval lateral sensilla styloconica response to fucose is 10 mM.
claims.source: The threshold concentrations for their responses to sucrose and fucose were 0.1 mM and 10 mM, respectively (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The medial sensilla styloconica of H. armigera larvae had a weak response to xylose.
claims.source: The medial sensilla styloconica had a weak response to xylose (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The mixture of 0.05 mM sucrose and 5 mM fucose induced higher responses than either compound alone in larval lateral sensilla styloconica.
claims.source: We also compared the responses of the lateral sensilla styloconica to 0.05 mM sucrose, 5 mM fucose, and their mixture with the same concentrations, and found that the mixture induced higher responses with only one amplitude spikes and a firing rate of 71±12.36 spikes/s, which was higher than the firing rates induced by 0.05 mM sucrose (39±6.37 spikes/s) and 5 mM fucose (36±8.87 spikes/s; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), confirming that the same cell responded to sucrose and fucose.
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The same cell in larval lateral sensilla styloconica responds to both sucrose and fucose.
claims.source: We also compared the responses of the lateral sensilla styloconica to 0.05 mM sucrose, 5 mM fucose, and their mixture with the same concentrations, and found that the mixture induced higher responses with only one amplitude spikes and a firing rate of 71±12.36 spikes/s, which was higher than the firing rates induced by 0.05 mM sucrose (39±6.37 spikes/s) and 5 mM fucose (36±8.87 spikes/s; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), confirming that the same cell responded to sucrose and fucose.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the mixture experiment showing only one spike amplitude.

claims.claim: There is only one GSN sensitive to sucrose and fucose in each maxillary galea of H. armigera larvae.
claims.source: We conclude that there is only one GSN sensitive to sucrose and fucose in each maxillary galea of larvae.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the electrophysiological data showing single-cell responses.

claims.claim: The contact chemosensilla on adult female antennae responded to sucrose, fucose, and fructose positively.
claims.source: The antennal sensilla responded to sucrose, fucose, and fructose positively (Figure 1C), the tarsal sensilla only responded to sucrose and fucose (Figure 1E), and the proboscis sensilla responded to sucrose, fucose, and fructose (Figure 1G), but their firing rates were between 9 and 22 spikes/s.
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The contact chemosensilla on adult female tarsi only responded to sucrose and fucose.
claims.source: The antennal sensilla responded to sucrose, fucose, and fructose positively (Figure 1C), the tarsal sensilla only responded to sucrose and fucose (Figure 1E), and the proboscis sensilla responded to sucrose, fucose, and fructose (Figure 1G), but their firing rates were between 9 and 22 spikes/s.
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: The contact chemosensilla on adult female proboscis responded to sucrose, fucose, and fructose.
claims.source: The antennal sensilla responded to sucrose, fucose, and fructose positively (Figure 1C), the tarsal sensilla only responded to sucrose and fucose (Figure 1E), and the proboscis sensilla responded to sucrose, fucose, and fructose (Figure 1G), but their firing rates were between 9 and 22 spikes/s.
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: The threshold concentrations of sucrose, fucose and fructose for adult antennal sensilla were all 10 mM.
claims.source: The dose–response curves showed that the threshold concentrations of sucrose, fucose and fructose were all 10 mM for the antennal sensilla (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), 100 mM, 10 mM and 100 mM for the tarsal sensilla (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), and 10 mM, 100 mM and 10 mM for the proboscis sensilla, respectively (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: The threshold concentrations of sucrose, fucose and fructose for adult tarsal sensilla were 100 mM, 10 mM and 100 mM respectively.
claims.source: The dose–response curves showed that the threshold concentrations of sucrose, fucose and fructose were all 10 mM for the antennal sensilla (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), 100 mM, 10 mM and 100 mM for the tarsal sensilla (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), and 10 mM, 100 mM and 10 mM for the proboscis sensilla, respectively (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: The threshold concentrations of sucrose, fucose and fructose for adult proboscis sensilla were 10 mM, 100 mM and 10 mM respectively.
claims.source: The dose–response curves showed that the threshold concentrations of sucrose, fucose and fructose were all 10 mM for the antennal sensilla (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), 100 mM, 10 mM and 100 mM for the tarsal sensilla (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), and 10 mM, 100 mM and 10 mM for the proboscis sensilla, respectively (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: The sugar GSNs of H. armigera larvae were 100-1,000 times more sensitive to sucrose than those of adults.
claims.source: The GSNs of larvae were 100–1,000 times more sensitive to sucrose than those of adults.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from comparing threshold concentrations between larvae (0.1 mM) and adults (10-100 mM).

claims.claim: Sucrose and fructose stimulated larval feeding at 10 mM.
claims.source: Sucrose and fructose stimulated larval feeding, and their threshold concentrations were 10 mM (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1); other tested sugars had no effect on larval feeding (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by two-choice feeding test data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claims.claim: The threshold concentration for larval feeding stimulation by sucrose and fructose is 10 mM.
claims.source: Sucrose and fructose stimulated larval feeding, and their threshold concentrations were 10 mM (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1); other tested sugars had no effect on larval feeding (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by two-choice feeding test data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claims.claim: Arabinose, fucose, galactose, glucose, trehalose, and xylose had no effect on larval feeding at 10 mM.
claims.source: Sucrose and fructose stimulated larval feeding, and their threshold concentrations were 10 mM (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1); other tested sugars had no effect on larval feeding (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by two-choice feeding test data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Antennal stimulation with 100 mM sucrose, fucose and fructose induced PER percentages of 64±4.35%, 44±5.96% and 20±1.92% respectively in adult females.
claims.source: The results showed that the PER percentage reached 64 ± 4.35%, 44 ± 5.96% and 20 ± 1.92% when the antennal sensilla were stimulated with sucrose, fucose and fructose (Figure 2C), while the PER percentage reached 53 ± 14.08%, 45 ± 4.44% and 36 ± 10.19% when the tarsal sensilla were stimulated, respectively (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by PER test data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Tarsal stimulation with 100 mM sucrose, fucose and fructose induced PER percentages of 53±14.08%, 45±4.44% and 36±10.19% respectively in adult females.
claims.source: The results showed that the PER percentage reached 64 ± 4.35%, 44 ± 5.96% and 20 ± 1.92% when the antennal sensilla were stimulated with sucrose, fucose and fructose (Figure 2C), while the PER percentage reached 53 ± 14.08%, 45 ± 4.44% and 36 ± 10.19% when the tarsal sensilla were stimulated, respectively (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by PER test data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Stimulation of antennal or tarsal sensilla by arabinose, galactose, glucose, trehalose, and xylose did not induce changes in PER percentage compared with water.
claims.source: Stimulation of the antennal or tarsal sensilla by other sugars did not induce changes in the PER percentage compared with stimulation of water (Figure 2C–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by PER test data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claims.claim: The threshold concentrations of sucrose, fucose, and fructose for antennal sensilla PER were 100 mM, 100 mM, and 1000 mM respectively.
claims.source: The dose–response curves showed that the threshold concentrations of sucrose, fucose, and fructose for the antennal sensilla were 100 mM, 100 mM, and 1000 mM (Figure 2E), those for the tarsal sensilla were 10 mM, 10 mM, and 100 mM, respectively (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by dose-response PER data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The threshold concentrations of sucrose, fucose, and fructose for tarsal sensilla PER were 10 mM, 10 mM, and 100 mM respectively.
claims.source: The dose–response curves showed that the threshold concentrations of sucrose, fucose, and fructose for the antennal sensilla were 100 mM, 100 mM, and 1000 mM (Figure 2E), those for the tarsal sensilla were 10 mM, 10 mM, and 100 mM, respectively (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by dose-response PER data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Nine putative sugar GR genes (Gr4-12) were validated in H. armigera.
claims.source: All nine putative sugar GR genes in H. armigera, Gr4–12 were validated, and their full-length cDNA sequences were cloned (The GenBank accession number is provided in Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by gene cloning experiments.

claims.claim: All putative sugar GRs of H. armigera were in the sugar GR clade except for HarmGr9, which was in the fructose GR clade.
claims.source: The phylogenetic analysis showed that candidate sugar GRs of these nine insect species grouped within two clades, the sugar GR clade and the fructose GR clade. All the putative sugar GRs of H. armigera were in the sugar GR clade except for HarmGr9, which was in the fructose GR clade (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Gr10 was highly expressed in the larval maxillary galea.
claims.source: Among all sugar GRs, Gr10 was highly expressed in the larval maxillary galea, whereas Gr6 was highly expressed in the antennae, tarsi, and proboscis of both male and female adults.
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Gr6 was highly expressed in the antennae, tarsi, and proboscis of both male and female adults.
claims.source: Among all sugar GRs, Gr10 was highly expressed in the larval maxillary galea, whereas Gr6 was highly expressed in the antennae, tarsi, and proboscis of both male and female adults.
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 3C-E.

claims.claim: Gr5 expression levels were highest in the proboscis followed by the tarsi, but very low in the antennae and the maxillary galea of larvae.
claims.source: Gr5 expression levels greatly varied; they were highest in the proboscis followed by the tarsi, but very low in the antennae and the maxillary galea of the larvae (Figure 3B–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 3B-E.

claims.claim: Oocytes expressing Gr10 only responded to sucrose with a current value of 4.10±0.53 μA.
claims.source: The results showed that the oocytes expressing Gr10 only responded to sucrose with a current value of 4.10±0.53 μA (Figure 4A–B); the oocytes expressing Gr6 showed responses to fucose and sucrose with a current value of 1.59±0.08 μA and 0.24±0.03 μA, respectively (Figure 4A–B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by two-electrode voltage-clamp data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claims.claim: Oocytes expressing Gr6 showed responses to fucose and sucrose with current values of 1.59±0.08 μA and 0.24±0.03 μA, respectively.
claims.source: The results showed that the oocytes expressing Gr10 only responded to sucrose with a current value of 4.10±0.53 μA (Figure 4A–B); the oocytes expressing Gr6 showed responses to fucose and sucrose with a current value of 1.59±0.08 μA and 0.24±0.03 μA, respectively (Figure 4A–B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by two-electrode voltage-clamp data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claims.claim: Oocytes expressing Gr4, Gr5, Gr7, Gr8, Gr11, and Gr12 singly had no response to the tested sugars.
claims.source: The oocytes expressing remaining six sugar GR genes (Gr4, Gr5, Gr7, Gr8, Gr11, and Gr12) singly had no response to the tested sugars (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by two-electrode voltage-clamp data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claims.claim: The threshold concentration of sucrose for oocytes expressing Gr10 was 100 mM.
claims.source: The dose–response curves showed that the threshold concentration of sucrose for the oocytes expressing Gr10 was 100 mM (Figure 4C–D), whereas the threshold concentrations of sucrose and fucose for the oocytes expressing Gr6 were 250 mM and 100 mM, respectively, and 500 mM fructose could also induce an inward current (Figure 4C–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 4C-D.

claims.claim: The threshold concentrations of sucrose and fucose for oocytes expressing Gr6 were 250 mM and 100 mM, respectively.
claims.source: The dose–response curves showed that the threshold concentration of sucrose for the oocytes expressing Gr10 was 100 mM (Figure 4C–D), whereas the threshold concentrations of sucrose and fucose for the oocytes expressing Gr6 were 250 mM and 100 mM, respectively, and 500 mM fructose could also induce an inward current (Figure 4C–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 4C-D.

claims.claim: 500 mM fructose could induce an inward current in oocytes expressing Gr6.
claims.source: The dose–response curves showed that the threshold concentration of sucrose for the oocytes expressing Gr10 was 100 mM (Figure 4C–D), whereas the threshold concentrations of sucrose and fucose for the oocytes expressing Gr6 were 250 mM and 100 mM, respectively, and 500 mM fructose could also induce an inward current (Figure 4C–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 4C-D.

claims.claim: Oocytes co-expressing Gr10 and Gr6 significantly responded to sucrose at 100 mM with a current value of 1.89±0.58 μA.
claims.source: The results showed that the oocytes co-expressing Gr10 and Gr6 significantly responded to sucrose with a current value of 1.89±0.58 μA at 100 mM, a threshold concentration, and had a weak response to fucose with a threshold concentration of 250 mM (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by two-electrode voltage-clamp data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Oocytes co-expressing Gr10 and Gr6 had a weak response to fucose with a threshold concentration of 250 mM.
claims.source: The results showed that the oocytes co-expressing Gr10 and Gr6 significantly responded to sucrose with a current value of 1.89±0.58 μA at 100 mM, a threshold concentration, and had a weak response to fucose with a threshold concentration of 250 mM (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by two-electrode voltage-clamp data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Oocytes expressing Gr5 and Gr6 had responses to 100 mM fucose with a current value of 0.11±0.015 μA and to 100 mM sucrose with a current value of 0.03±0.002 μA.
claims.source: Similar to the oocytes expressing Gr6, the oocytes expressing Gr5 and Gr6 had responses to 100 mM fucose with a current value of 0.11±0.015 μA and to 100 mM sucrose with a current value of 0.03±0.002 μA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by two-electrode voltage-clamp data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C.

claims.claim: Gr10 and Gr6 are capable of forming functional receptors singly.
claims.source: These results indicate that Gr10 and Gr6 are capable of forming functional receptors singly, and the function of the two co-expressed receptors is not equal to the sum of the functions of the two receptors (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the oocyte expression data showing responses when expressed individually.

claims.claim: The function of Gr10 and Gr6 co-expressed receptors is not equal to the sum of the functions of the two receptors.
claims.source: These results indicate that Gr10 and Gr6 are capable of forming functional receptors singly, and the function of the two co-expressed receptors is not equal to the sum of the functions of the two receptors (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from comparing the responses of co-expressed receptors to individually expressed receptors.

claims.claim: Gr10-/- generated a 4 bp deletion at the sgRNA targeting site.
claims.source: Gr10-/- and Gr6-/- generated 4 bp and 17 bp deletions at the sgRNA targeting site (Figure 5), respectively, which also confirmed the deletion at the mRNA level in Gr10-/- and Gr6-/- (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Gr6-/- generated a 17 bp deletion at the sgRNA targeting site.
claims.source: Gr10-/- and Gr6-/- generated 4 bp and 17 bp deletions at the sgRNA targeting site (Figure 5), respectively, which also confirmed the deletion at the mRNA level in Gr10-/- and Gr6-/- (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The deletion in Gr10-/- resulted in a truncated Gr10 protein reduced from 460 to 62 amino acids containing no transmembrane domains.
claims.source: The deletion resulted in truncated Gr10 and Gr6 proteins. The Gr10 sequence was reduced from 460 to 62 amino acids and contained no transmembrane domains, whereas the Gr6 sequence was reduced from 452 to 115 amino acids and contained only two transmembrane domains (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is predicted from the sequence deletion and shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The deletion in Gr6-/- resulted in a truncated Gr6 protein reduced from 452 to 115 amino acids containing only two transmembrane domains.
claims.source: The deletion resulted in truncated Gr10 and Gr6 proteins. The Gr10 sequence was reduced from 460 to 62 amino acids and contained no transmembrane domains, whereas the Gr6 sequence was reduced from 452 to 115 amino acids and contained only two transmembrane domains (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is predicted from the sequence deletion and shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: The firing rates of larval sugar GSNs in Gr10-/- to 1 mM, 10 mM and 100 mM sucrose were only 40%, 20% and 28% of those in WT, respectively.
claims.source: To 1 mM, 10 mM and 100 mM sucrose, the firing rates of the larval sugar GSNs in Gr10-/- were only 40%, 20% and 28% of those in the WT, respectively, whereas those in Gr6-/- larvae did not differ from those in the WT larvae (Figure 6A–B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claims.claim: The firing rates of larval sugar GSNs in Gr6-/- to sucrose did not differ from those in WT larvae.
claims.source: To 1 mM, 10 mM and 100 mM sucrose, the firing rates of the larval sugar GSNs in Gr10-/- were only 40%, 20% and 28% of those in the WT, respectively, whereas those in Gr6-/- larvae did not differ from those in the WT larvae (Figure 6A–B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claims.claim: The firing rates of larval sugar GSNs in Gr6-/- to 10 mM and 100 mM fucose were only 20% and 5.8% of those in WT, respectively.
claims.source: To 10 mM and 100 mM fucose, the firing rates of the larval sugar GSNs in Gr6-/- were only 20% and 5.8% of those in the WT, respectively, whereas those of Gr10-/- did not differ from the WT (Figure 6A–B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claims.claim: The firing rates of larval sugar GSNs in Gr10-/- to fucose did not differ from WT.
claims.source: To 10 mM and 100 mM fucose, the firing rates of the larval sugar GSNs in Gr6-/- were only 20% and 5.8% of those in the WT, respectively, whereas those of Gr10-/- did not differ from the WT (Figure 6A–B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claims.claim: Gr10 plays a key role in sucrose reception in larval lateral sensilla styloconica.
claims.source: It is clear that Gr10 plays a key role in sucrose reception, whereas Gr6 plays a key role in fucose reception of the sugar GSNs in the lateral sensilla styloconica of larvae.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the knockout experiments showing reduced sucrose responses in Gr10-/-.

claims.claim: Gr6 plays a key role in fucose reception in larval lateral sensilla styloconica.
claims.source: It is clear that Gr10 plays a key role in sucrose reception, whereas Gr6 plays a key role in fucose reception of the sugar GSNs in the lateral sensilla styloconica of larvae.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the knockout experiments showing reduced fucose responses in Gr6-/-.

claims.claim: The firing rates of sugar GSNs in antennal sensilla of Gr6-/- to 10 mM and 100 mM sucrose were only 32% and 9% of those in WT, respectively.
claims.source: The firing rates of the sugar GSNs in the antennal sensilla of Gr6-/- to 10 mM and 100 mM sucrose, 10 mM and 100 mM fucose, and 100 mM fructose were only 32% and 9%, 22% and 11%, and 29% of those in the WT, respectively (Figure 6C–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6C-D.

claims.claim: The firing rates of sugar GSNs in antennal sensilla of Gr6-/- to 10 mM and 100 mM fucose were only 22% and 11% of those in WT, respectively.
claims.source: The firing rates of the sugar GSNs in the antennal sensilla of Gr6-/- to 10 mM and 100 mM sucrose, 10 mM and 100 mM fucose, and 100 mM fructose were only 32% and 9%, 22% and 11%, and 29% of those in the WT, respectively (Figure 6C–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6C-D.

claims.claim: The firing rates of sugar GSNs in antennal sensilla of Gr6-/- to 100 mM fructose were only 29% of those in WT.
claims.source: The firing rates of the sugar GSNs in the antennal sensilla of Gr6-/- to 10 mM and 100 mM sucrose, 10 mM and 100 mM fucose, and 100 mM fructose were only 32% and 9%, 22% and 11%, and 29% of those in the WT, respectively (Figure 6C–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6C-D.

claims.claim: The firing rates of sugar GSNs in antennal sensilla of Gr10-/- to sucrose, fucose, or fructose did not differ from those of WT adults.
claims.source: The firing rates of the sugar GSNs in antennal sensilla of Gr10-/- to sucrose, fucose, or fructose did not differ from those of the WT adults.
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6C-D.

claims.claim: The response patterns of sugar GSNs in foreleg tarsi of WT, Gr10-/-, and Gr6-/- to sugars were similar to those of sugar GSNs in antennae.
claims.source: The response patterns of the sugar GSNs in the foreleg tarsi of the WT, Gr10-/-, and Gr6-/- to 10 mM and 100 mM sucrose, 10 mM and 100 mM fucose, and 100 mM fructose were similar to those of the sugar GSNs in antennae (Figure 6E–F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6E-F.

claims.claim: The firing rates of sugar GSNs in proboscis sensilla of Gr6-/- to sucrose, fucose, and fructose were much lower and even close to zero.
claims.source: The firing rates of the sugar GSNs in proboscis sensilla of Gr6-/- to sucrose, fucose, and fructose were much lower and even close to zero (Figure 6G–H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6G-H.

claims.claim: The firing rates of sugar GSNs in tarsal and proboscis sensilla of Gr10-/- to sucrose, fucose, and fructose did not differ from those of WT adults.
claims.source: The firing rates of the sugar GSNs in tarsal and proboscis sensilla of Gr10-/- to sucrose, fucose, and fructose did not differ from those of the WT adults (Figure 6E–H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6E-H.

claims.claim: Gr10-/- larvae showed no preference for leaf discs painted with 10 mM sucrose.
claims.source: The Gr10-/- larvae showed no preference for the leaf discs painted with 10 mM sucrose (p=0.4258).
claims.evidence: This is supported by two-choice feeding test data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Gr10-/- larvae still had preference for discs with 100 mM sucrose though their PI value was decreased compared to WT.
claims.source: However, they still had preference for the discs with 100 mM sucrose (p=0.0141; Figure 7A–B) though their PI value was decreased than those of the WT (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by two-choice feeding test data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Gr6-/- larvae retained a significant preference for 10 mM or 100 mM sucrose diets.
claims.source: The Gr6-/- larvae were the same as the WT larvae and retained a significant preference for 10 mM or 100 mM sucrose diets (Figure 7A–B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by two-choice feeding test data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claims.claim: WT, Gr10-/-, and Gr6-/- larvae all showed similar preference for 10 mM and 100 mM fructose.
claims.source: The WT, Gr10-/-, and Gr6-/- larvae all showed similar preference for 10 mM and 100 mM fructose (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by two-choice feeding test data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B.

claims.claim: Gr10-/- larvae fed significantly less than WT larvae on cabbage leaves, corn kernels, pea seeds, pepper fruits, and tomato fruits.
claims.source: On each of these plant tissues, the Gr10-/- larvae fed significantly less than the WT larvae, but the Gr6-/- larvae fed the same amount as the WT larvae (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by no-choice feeding test data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Gr6-/- larvae fed the same amount as WT larvae on cabbage leaves, corn kernels, pea seeds, pepper fruits, and tomato fruits.
claims.source: On each of these plant tissues, the Gr10-/- larvae fed significantly less than the WT larvae, but the Gr6-/- larvae fed the same amount as the WT larvae (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by no-choice feeding test data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Gr6-/- females showed a considerably lower PER percentage than WT females when antennae or tarsi were stimulated with sucrose, fucose, or fructose.
claims.source: When antennae or tarsi were stimulated with 10 mM, 100 mM, or 1000 mM sucrose, fucose, or fructose, Gr6-/- females showed a considerably lower PER percentage than the WT females and even had little or no PER in response to sucrose and fucose, whereas the PER percentage of Gr10-/- females was not different from that of the WT females (Figure 7D–I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by PER test data shown in Figure 7D-I.

claims.claim: The PER percentage of Gr10-/- females was not different from that of WT females when antennae or tarsi were stimulated with sucrose, fucose, or fructose.
claims.source: When antennae or tarsi were stimulated with 10 mM, 100 mM, or 1000 mM sucrose, fucose, or fructose, Gr6-/- females showed a considerably lower PER percentage than the WT females and even had little or no PER in response to sucrose and fucose, whereas the PER percentage of Gr10-/- females was not different from that of the WT females (Figure 7D–I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by PER test data shown in Figure 7D-I.

claims.claim: Gr10 mediates the feeding preference of larvae to sucrose.
claims.source: In conclusion, Gr10 plays a key role in sucrose reception by the sugar GSNs in the larval lateral sensilla styloconica, and mediates the feeding preference of larvae to sucrose, whereas Gr6 plays a key role in sensing sucrose, fucose, and fructose by the sugar GSNs in contact chemosensilla of the adult antennae, foreleg tarsi and proboscis, and mediates the related PER behavior of adults.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the combined electrophysiological and behavioral data from knockout experiments.

claims.claim: Gr6 mediates the PER behavior of adults in response to sucrose, fucose, and fructose.
claims.source: In conclusion, Gr10 plays a key role in sucrose reception by the sugar GSNs in the larval lateral sensilla styloconica, and mediates the feeding preference of larvae to sucrose, whereas Gr6 plays a key role in sensing sucrose, fucose, and fructose by the sugar GSNs in contact chemosensilla of the adult antennae, foreleg tarsi and proboscis, and mediates the related PER behavior of adults.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the combined electrophysiological and behavioral data from knockout experiments.

claims.claim: H. armigera larvae and adults adopt different sugar-sensing systems to satisfy their requirements for food selection.
claims.source: Our findings indicate that the H. armigera larvae and adults adopt different sugar-sensing systems to satisfy their requirements for food selection.

results.result: Larval lateral sensilla styloconica show high sensitivity to sucrose with a threshold of 0.1 mM, which is 100-1000 times more sensitive than adult sensilla. A single gustatory sensory neuron (GSN) in each maxillary galea responds to both sucrose and fucose, as demonstrated by mixture experiments showing only one spike amplitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C42 and C49 are well-supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 1A-B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D. The threshold concentrations are clearly determined from dose-response curves, and the single-cell nature is confirmed by spike amplitude analysis. The 100-1000-fold sensitivity difference is calculated from comparing larval (0.1 mM) versus adult (10-100 mM) thresholds.

results.result: Adult contact chemosensilla on antennae, tarsi, and proboscis respond to sugars with lower sensitivity than larvae. Antennal sensilla respond to sucrose, fucose, and fructose (all 10 mM threshold), tarsal sensilla respond to sucrose and fucose (100 mM and 10 mM thresholds), and proboscis sensilla respond to sucrose, fucose, and fructose (10 mM, 100 mM, and 10 mM thresholds).
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C48 are supported by comprehensive electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1C-H with dose-response curves. The data clearly demonstrate differential sugar responses across adult organs with appropriate controls (KCl) and statistical analysis. Sample sizes are adequate (n=15-21).

results.result: Larval feeding behavior shows that sucrose and fructose stimulate feeding with a threshold of 10 mM, while arabinose, fucose, galactose, glucose, trehalose, and xylose have no effect on larval feeding at 10 mM.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C52 are supported by two-choice feeding test data in Figure 2A-B with appropriate statistical analysis (paired t-test, n=20). The preference index values clearly distinguish active sugars from inactive ones, with proper controls.

results.result: Adult proboscis extension reflex (PER) is induced by sucrose, fucose, and fructose stimulation of antennae and tarsi, with varying threshold concentrations. Antennal stimulation thresholds are 100 mM, 100 mM, and 1000 mM for sucrose, fucose, and fructose respectively, while tarsal stimulation thresholds are 10 mM, 10 mM, and 100 mM.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C57 are supported by PER test data in Figure 2C-F with dose-response curves and appropriate statistical analysis. The experiments include proper controls (water) and adequate replication (n=3 with 20-30 individuals per replicate). The differential sensitivity between organs is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Nine putative sugar GR genes (Gr4-12) were validated and phylogenetically analyzed. Gr10 is highly expressed in larval maxillary galea, while Gr6 is highly expressed in adult antennae, tarsi, and proboscis. All H. armigera sugar GRs cluster in the sugar GR clade except HarmGr9, which is in the fructose GR clade.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C62 are supported by gene cloning data, phylogenetic analysis (Figure 3A), and qRT-PCR expression data (Figure 3B-E). The phylogenetic tree includes appropriate bootstrap values (>95% for key nodes), and expression data includes proper normalization (18S rRNA) and statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA with Tukey's HSD, n=3).

results.result: Xenopus oocyte expression experiments show that Gr10 specifically responds to sucrose (threshold 100 mM), while Gr6 responds to fucose (threshold 100 mM), sucrose (threshold 250 mM), and weakly to fructose (500 mM). Other sugar GRs (Gr4, Gr5, Gr7, Gr8, Gr11, Gr12) showed no response when expressed individually.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C68 are supported by two-electrode voltage-clamp data in Figure 4A-D with dose-response curves. The experiments include appropriate controls (water-injected oocytes, Ringer solution) and adequate sample sizes (n=3-20 depending on receptor). The specificity of Gr10 for sucrose and broader response profile of Gr6 are clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Co-expression of Gr10 and Gr6 in Xenopus oocytes produces responses to sucrose (threshold 100 mM) and weak responses to fucose (threshold 250 mM). The functional properties of co-expressed receptors are not equal to the sum of individually expressed receptors, indicating both receptors can form functional receptors independently.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C73 are supported by voltage-clamp data in Figure 4. The non-additive nature of co-expression is demonstrated by comparing current values: Gr10 alone (4.10 μA), Gr6 alone (0.24 μA for sucrose), but co-expression (1.89 μA) is not equal to their sum. This suggests complex receptor interactions rather than simple additive effects.

results.result: CRISPR/Cas9 generated homozygous mutants Gr10-/- (4 bp deletion) and Gr6-/- (17 bp deletion) at sgRNA targeting sites, resulting in truncated proteins. Gr10 protein is reduced from 460 to 62 amino acids with no transmembrane domains, while Gr6 protein is reduced from 452 to 115 amino acids with only two transmembrane domains.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 are supported by sequencing data (Figure 5), mRNA confirmation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and protein structure predictions (Figure 5C, F). The deletions are confirmed at both DNA and mRNA levels. Off-target analysis was performed and no off-target effects were detected (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).

results.result: Gr10 knockout dramatically reduces larval sucrose responses (to 20-40% of WT) but not fucose responses, while Gr6 knockout dramatically reduces larval fucose responses (to 5.8-20% of WT) but not sucrose responses. This demonstrates that Gr10 plays a key role in sucrose reception and Gr6 plays a key role in fucose reception in larval lateral sensilla styloconica.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C83 are supported by electrophysiological recordings from knockout mutants (Figure 6A-B) with appropriate controls (sinigrin responses unchanged) and statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA with Tukey's post-hoc, n=12-13). The differential effects on sucrose versus fucose responses clearly demonstrate receptor-specific functions.

results.result: Gr6 knockout dramatically reduces adult sugar responses across all tested organs (antennae, tarsi, proboscis) to sucrose, fucose, and fructose (to 9-32% of WT), while Gr10 knockout has no effect on adult sugar responses. The response patterns are similar across antennae and tarsi, with proboscis showing the most dramatic reduction in Gr6-/- mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C90 are supported by comprehensive electrophysiological recordings from adult organs in knockout mutants (Figure 6C-H) with appropriate controls (nicotine responses unchanged) and statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA, n=14-20). The organ-specific expression pattern of Gr6 correlates with the knockout phenotypes.

results.result: Gr10-/- larvae show no preference for 10 mM sucrose but retain preference for 100 mM sucrose (though reduced), and feed significantly less on various plant tissues (cabbage, corn, pea, pepper, tomato). Gr6-/- larvae retain normal sucrose preference and feeding behavior. Both mutants show normal fructose preference.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C96 are supported by two-choice feeding tests (Figure 7A-B) and no-choice feeding tests (Figure 7C) with appropriate statistical analysis (paired t-test for two-choice, one-way ANOVA for no-choice, n=20). The residual response to high sucrose in Gr10-/- is consistent with low-level Gr6 expression in larvae, as discussed by the authors.

results.result: Gr6-/- females show dramatically reduced PER to sucrose, fucose, and fructose when antennae or tarsi are stimulated, while Gr10-/- females show normal PER. This demonstrates that Gr10 mediates larval feeding preference to sucrose, while Gr6 mediates adult PER behavior in response to multiple sugars.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C100 are supported by PER test data from knockout mutants (Figure 7D-I) with dose-response curves and appropriate statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA, n=3 with 20-30 individuals per replicate). The behavioral phenotypes correlate well with the electrophysiological data and expression patterns.

results.result: H. armigera larvae and adults use differential gustatory receptors (Gr10 in larvae for low sucrose detection, Gr6 in adults for higher sucrose and other saccharides) to sense sucrose, resulting in 100-1000-fold sensitivity differences. This represents an evolutionary adaptation to different food sources with varying sugar types and concentrations throughout the life cycle.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C11-C14, C101, C106, and C142 represent the main conclusions synthesized from all experimental data (electrophysiology, expression, functional analysis, knockout phenotypes). The evolutionary interpretation is well-supported by the ecological context (larvae feed on plant tissues with lower sucrose, adults feed on nectar with higher sugar concentrations) and the functional data demonstrating differential receptor usage.

results.result: Low-level expressed Gr6 likely contributes to residual sucrose responses in Gr10-/- larvae, and fructose-tuned GRs other than Gr6 (likely Gr9) contribute to residual fructose responses in Gr6-/- adults. Gr10 and Gr6 are co-expressed in larval GSNs at different levels, with Gr10 primarily determining sucrose sensitivity and Gr6 functional for fucose detection.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C116 represent mechanistic interpretations supported by: (1) residual responses in knockout mutants (Figure 6-7), (2) expression data showing low Gr6 in larvae (Figure 3B), (3) oocyte co-expression data (Figure 4), and (4) known function of Gr9 as a fructose receptor (C110). The interpretations are logical and consistent with all experimental observations.

results.result: The sugar content varies dramatically between larval food sources (tomato leaves: 13.72-42.06 mM sucrose; tomato fruits: 35.2-988.22 mM) and adult food sources (cotton nectar: 0.5-1.7 M; soybean nectar: 1.2-3 M). Using value-based and target-specific sugar-sensing systems is proposed as a favorable evolutionary choice for phytophagous insects.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C105 are supported by citations to published literature (Schauer et al., 2005; Vansell, 1944; Waller et al., 1981; Free, 1993). Claim C107 is a speculative evolutionary interpretation, but it is well-grounded in the ecological context and the experimental findings demonstrating differential receptor usage. The interpretation is reasonable but represents speculation rather than direct experimental evidence.

results.result: The eight sugar GR genes (except Gr9) are tandemly duplicated on the same genomic scaffold. There is differential expression of Gr5 and Gr6 among adult taste organs (antennae, tarsi, proboscis), which may reflect evolutionary adaptation and functional differentiation in foraging behavior.
results.evaluation: Claim C136 is supported by genome data analysis (Pearce et al., 2017). Claims C138-C140 are supported by expression data (Figure 3C-E) showing organ-specific patterns. Claims C137 and C139 represent speculative evolutionary interpretations citing Delventhal and Carlson, 2016. While the expression patterns are clearly demonstrated, the evolutionary interpretations are reasonable but speculative.

results.result: Phylogenetic analysis shows Gr10 clusters with BmorGr5 and Gr6 clusters with BmorGr6 of Bombyx mori. Similar GRs are found in other Lepidopteran species (D. plexippus, H. melpomene, P. xylostella), suggesting similar sugar-sensing mechanisms may exist in other Lepidoptera.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C145 are supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 3A) with appropriate bootstrap support. Claim C146 is speculation based on phylogenetic relationships, which is reasonable but requires experimental verification in other species. The phylogenetic analysis is sound, but the functional inference across species is speculative.

results.result: Knocking out Gr10 or Gr6 is unlikely to be compensated by overexpression of other sugar GRs, as shown by previous work demonstrating that Orco knockout had no significant effect on most chemoreceptor gene expression in H. armigera.
results.evaluation: Claim C111 is an inference from the observed knockout phenotypes showing persistent deficits. Claim C112 cites Fan et al., 2022 showing lack of compensatory expression changes in a different knockout. While the inference is reasonable, direct measurement of sugar GR expression levels in Gr10-/- and Gr6-/- mutants would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Knockout of Gr10 or Gr6 leads to decreased sugar sensitivity and food preference, which is proposed to bring adverse consequences to insect survival and reproduction. Studying sugar perception mechanisms may provide new means for agricultural pest control by targeting sugar receptors.
results.evaluation: Claim C147 is well-supported by experimental data (Figures 6-7). However, claims C148 and C149 are speculative. No fitness measurements (survival, reproduction, development time) were directly assessed in the knockout mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C shows no differences in body weight, lifespan, or egg number, though these may not capture field fitness). The pest control application is speculative and would require extensive additional work.

results.result: Background and context claims establishing the importance of sugar reception in herbivorous insects, the pest status of H. armigera, the distribution of sugar-sensitive neurons in Lepidoptera, and the knowledge gap regarding molecular mechanisms of sugar reception in Lepidopteran insects.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5, C15-C23, C28-C35, C117-C118, and C141 represent background knowledge and context, supported by appropriate citations to published literature. These establish the scientific rationale for the study and are generally accepted facts in the field. Claim C141 about novelty is supported by the literature review showing no prior reports of sucrose receptor mechanisms in Lepidopteran external taste neurons.

results.result: Comparative biology of sugar reception across animals, including mammals (T1R2/T1R3), Drosophila (multiple GRs including Gr5a, Gr64a, Gr64f, Gr43a), honeybees (AmGr1-3), whiteflies (BtabGr1), and other Lepidoptera (BmGr4, BmGr9, orthologs in other species).
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27, C119-C135 represent comparative biology context, all supported by appropriate citations to published literature. These establish the broader context of sugar reception mechanisms across taxa and provide the comparative framework for interpreting the H. armigera findings. All citations appear appropriate and accurate.

results.result: Larval sugar sensory neurons in maxillary galea are 100-1000 times more sensitive to sucrose than adult neurons in antennae, tarsi, and proboscis, with larvae showing threshold responses at 0.1 mM sucrose compared to 10-100 mM in adults. The lateral sensilla styloconica contain a single GSN responding to both sucrose and fucose.
results.evaluation: All reviewers describe the data as 'convincing' (Reviewer 1) and note the study employed comprehensive electrophysiology techniques (Reviewer 2). No concerns were raised about the differential sensitivity findings or the characterization of larval versus adult sensory responses.

results.result: Gr10 is highly expressed in larval maxillary galea and Gr6 is highly expressed in adult antennae, tarsi, and proboscis, with differential expression patterns across taste organs. Gr5 shows variable expression highest in proboscis.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the comprehensive gene expression analysis using qRT-PCR. Reviewer 2 notes the study 'employed electrophysiology, ectopic expression of Grs in Xenopus, genome editing, and behavioral studies' as strengths, implicitly supporting the expression data.

results.result: Xenopus oocyte expression experiments show Gr10 responds specifically to sucrose while Gr6 responds to fucose, sucrose, and fructose. Both receptors can function independently, and co-expression does not produce additive responses.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 specifically highlights 'ectopic expression of Grs in Xenopus' as a strength supporting the differential specificity findings. Reviewer 1 states the data are 'convincing,' and no concerns were raised about the oocyte expression system results.

results.result: CRISPR/Cas9 knockout of Gr10 resulted in 4 bp deletion producing truncated protein and significantly reduced larval sucrose responses (to 20-40% of WT), while Gr6 knockout (17 bp deletion) reduced larval fucose responses (to 5.8-20% of WT) but not sucrose responses.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly notes 'genome editing' as a strength of the study. Reviewer 1 describes the data as 'convincing.' No reviewer questioned the knockout phenotypes or the conclusion that Gr10 mediates larval sucrose detection while Gr6 mediates fucose detection.

results.result: In adults, Gr6 knockout dramatically reduced responses to sucrose, fucose, and fructose in antennae (to 9-32% of WT), tarsi, and proboscis (near zero), while Gr10 knockout had no effect on adult sugar responses.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the genetic analysis as showing 'stage specific functions in sugar perception' (Reviewer 3). The comprehensive electrophysiological characterization across multiple adult organs is implicitly supported by Reviewer 2's acknowledgment of the breadth of techniques.

results.result: Behavioral feeding assays show Gr10-/- larvae lost preference for 10 mM sucrose and fed significantly less on plant tissues, while maintaining some response to 100 mM sucrose. Gr6-/- larvae showed normal feeding behavior. Both genotypes responded normally to fructose.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 specifically highlights 'behavioral studies on insects' as a strength. Reviewer 3 notes the study assessed 'behavioral responses in larva and adult,' and no concerns were raised about the feeding assay results or their interpretation.

results.result: Adult proboscis extension reflex (PER) assays show Gr6-/- females had considerably lower PER to sucrose, fucose, and fructose when antennae or tarsi were stimulated, while Gr10-/- females showed normal PER responses.
results.evaluation: The behavioral PER data are part of the comprehensive behavioral analysis praised by Reviewer 2. Reviewer 1's statement that 'the data are convincing' encompasses these behavioral findings, and no specific concerns were raised.

results.result: The study concludes that Gr10 mediates larval detection of lower sucrose concentrations while Gr6 mediates adult detection of higher sucrose and other saccharides, representing stage-specific sugar-sensing systems adapted to different food sources with different sugar compositions.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states the authors 'find that the larval and adult forms utilise different receptors to sense sugars' and calls this an 'important study.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'Gr10 and Gr6 genes provide stage specific functions in sugar perception.' This central conclusion is fully endorsed.

results.result: Nine putative sugar GR genes (Gr4-12) were validated and phylogenetically analyzed, showing all except Gr9 cluster in the sugar GR clade. Gr10 clusters with BmorGr5 and Gr6 with BmorGr6, with related GRs found in other Lepidopteran species.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes the authors 'used phylogenetics and gene expression (RNAseq) to identify candidates for sugar reception' as part of the study design. No concerns were raised about the phylogenetic analysis or gene identification.

results.result: The authors infer that low-level Gr6 expression likely accounts for residual sucrose responses in Gr10-/- larvae, that other fructose-tuned GRs contribute to adult fructose detection, and that Gr10 and Gr6 are co-expressed in larval GSNs at different levels determining response profiles.
results.evaluation: These mechanistic interpretations follow logically from the knockout phenotypes and expression data. Reviewer 2 notes the study provides 'fundamental understanding of the gustation process,' implicitly accepting these interpretations. No reviewer challenged these inferences.

results.result: The sugar GR genes form a tandem cluster on the same genomic scaffold, and differential expression of Gr5 and Gr6 across adult taste organs may reflect evolutionary adaptation and functional differentiation in foraging behavior.
results.evaluation: The genomic organization and expression patterns are presented as data without reviewer objection. Reviewer 2 notes the study advances 'comprehension of lepidopteran insect biology, gustation, and feeding behavior,' supporting these evolutionary interpretations.

results.result: The authors speculate that similar sugar-sensing mechanisms may exist in other Lepidopteran species, that reduced sugar sensitivity would have adverse consequences for survival, and that these findings may provide new pest control strategies.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states the findings 'will be of interest to neuroscientists working in sensory coding of sugars and to the pest management field,' directly endorsing the applied implications. The speculation about other species is reasonable given the phylogenetic data.

results.result: The study addresses a knowledge gap by providing the first report of the molecular basis of sucrose reception in external taste neurons of a Lepidopteran insect, as this remained unclear despite extensive work in mammals and Drosophila.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 calls this an 'important study' that identifies gustatory receptors for sugar sensing. Reviewer 2 states it 'holds significant importance in advancing our comprehension of lepidopteran insect biology.' The novelty claim is fully endorsed.
